sidenotes.text: Gorgias.
Gorgias is ready to answer all comers.
Polus offers to take the place of Gorgias in the argument.
The question is asked, ‘What is Gorgias?’
Gorgias supersedes Polus.
Answer:—Gorgias is one of the best proficients in the noblest art.
This is no answer.
Better:—Gorgias is a rhetorician and a teacher of rhetoric.
The admirable brevity of Gorgias.
And rhetoric is concerned with discourse.
How is rhetoric distinguished from more special arts?
But so are all the other arts.
You mean to say that rhetoric belongs to that class of arts which is chiefly concerned with words.
Rhetoric and arithmetic.
And yet you would not call arithmetic rhetoric.
Illustrations.
The old drinking song.
Rhetoric has to do with words: about the greatest and best of human things.
But which are they?
Gorgias is brought to the point.
Freedom and power, and the word which gives them.
Rhetoric is the art of persuading, says Gorgias.
Socrates insists on taking ‘one step at a time.’
But so is arithmetic, so is painting.
Knowledge and belief.
Of what persuasion is rhetoric the artificer?
Of persuasion in the courts and assemblies about the just and unjust.
Knowledge and belief are not the same things; for there may be a false belief, but not a false knowledge.
What do we really mean concerning rhetoric?
And rhetoric is only the creator of a belief, but gives no instruction.
Neither is the rhetorician taken into counsel when anything has to be done.
Gorgias and his brother Herodicus.
But, says Gorgias, he will persuade people to do it.
The rhetorician more than a match for a man of any other profession.
The apology of Gorgias.
His pupils may make a bad use of his instructions, but he is not to be blamed for this.
If Gorgias, like Socrates, is one of those who rejoice in being refuted, he would like to cross-examine him; if not, not.
The inconsistency of Gorgias.
Delight of the audience at the prospect of an argument.
The rhetorician need only know appearance.
The rhetorician has greater powers of persuasion with the mob than e. g. the physician.
The more ignorant therefore will have more power than he who knows.
The false analogy of the arts.
And is the rhetorician as ignorant of good and evil, just and unjust, as about special arts; or will Gorgias teach him these things first?
He must be taught.
The inconsistency of Gorgias pointed out.

He who has learned what is just, is admitted to be just and to act justly. But if so, the rhetorician, having learned what is just, must act justly, and can never therefore make an ill use of rhetoric.
A change in the parts.
The paradoxes of Socrates arouse the ire of Polus.
Socrates is willing enough to receive his correction, if he will only be brief.
‘Am I to be deprived of speech in a free state?’
‘Am I to be compelled to listen?’
Socrates asks instead of answering.
Socrates in his answer contrives to give Polus a lesson.
Once more, ‘What is rhetoric?’
He puts rhetoric and cookery in the same class; and that class is flattery.
Shams and flatteries.
Rhetoric is the shadow of a part of politics.
‘But what in the world does this mean?’
Returning to first principles, Socrates assumes the existence of souls and bodies which may or may not be in a good condition, real or apparent.

To the soul corresponds the art of politics which has two parts, legislation and justice, and to the body corresponds another nameless art of training which has two parts, medicine and gymnastic; and these four have four shams corresponding to them.
Rhetoric and Sophistic.
The shams are cooking, dressing up, sophistry, rhetoric.
Hard words pass between Polus and Socrates.
Socrates excuses himself for the length at which he has spoken.
Polus cannot be made to understand that rhetoricians have no real power in a state, because they do not do what they ultimately will, but only what they think best.
Polus is greatly irritated by Socrates.
For a fool and a flatterer cannot know what is good.
What men will is not what they think best.
A man cannot will unless he knows the ultimate good for the sake of which he acts.
Good is the end of human action.
Will is the correlative of good.
No man does what he wills who does what is evil.
He who makes a bad use of power is not to be envied, but pitied.
A paradox.
Better to suffer than to do injustice.
A tyrant has no real power any more than a man who runs out into the Agora carrying a dagger.
Is Archelaus happy?
Even what we commonly call the evils of life may be goods in disguise.
Is the great king happy?
Certainly not, if he is wicked.
Polus attempts to prove the happiness of the unjust by the story of Archelaus, who has lately by many crimes gained the throne of Macedonia.
Socrates sees no force in such arguments.
Socrates alone in his opinion.
The multitude of witnesses are nothing to him.
He must convince his opponent and himself by argument.
A greater paradox than the last;
According to Polus the unjust man may be happy if he is unpunished: Socrates maintains that he is more happy, or less unhappy, if he meets with retribution.
which Polus begins by laughing at;
What nonsense! Do you mean that the man who expires among tortures is happier than the successful tyrant?
Neither is to be called happy if both are wicked.
Why refute what nobody believes? Ask the company.
Socrates never could count heads. This is his description of one of the noblest actions of his life.
Say rather, why affirm what every body knows?
but ends by acknowledging the truth of it.
Polus, while denying that to do injustice is worse than to suffer, acknowledges it to be more disgraceful. Hence the shipwreck of his argument.
The standard of utility.
All things may be measured by the standard of pleasure and utility or of pain and evil.
If to do is, as Polus admits, more disgraceful than to endure wrong, it must also be more evil.
The two sorts of refutation.
Polus is refuted out of his own mouth.
The next question: Is it better for the guilty to suffer or not to suffer punishment?
Correspondence of suffering and action.

Since the affection of the patient answers to the act of the agent, it follows that he who is punished justly suffers justly, and therefore honourably, and is delivered from the greatest of all evils, the evil of the soul, which, being the most disgraceful, is also the most painful or hurtful.
Sophistry of Socrates.
Analogy of soul and body.
Polus stumbles at the notion which he has already admitted, that the evil of the soul is more painful than that of the body.
The judge and the physician.
Punishment is the deliverance from evil, and he who is punished, like him who is healed, is happier than he who is not punished or not healed.
Happiest of all is he who is just; happy in the second degree he who is delivered from injustice by punishment, most deluded and most unhappy of all he who lives on, enjoying the fruit of his crimes.
The escape from punishment an evil.
The case of Archelaus regarded in a new light.
Archelaus then is more miserable than his victims.
Injustice, if not removed, will become the cancer of the soul.
The only use of rhetoric is that it enables a man to expose his own injustice and to petition for speedy punishment.
Of what use then is rhetoric?
A slighter and secondary use of rhetoric in self-defence against an enemy, or in preventing the punishment of an enemy.
Is Socrates in earnest?
Callicles asks in amazement whether Socrates really means what he says.
I am only repeating the words of philosophy, whose lover I am. For as you love the Athenian people and their namesake Demus, so I have two loves, philosophy and Alcibiades.
The son of Cleinias is inconstant, but philosophy is ever the same: she it is whom you have to refute: I am only her mouth-piece.
Polus and Callicles.
Polus was vanquished because he refused to take a bold line.
Callicles would return to the rule of nature in the lower sense of the term.
Convention was only introduced by the weak majority in order to protect themselves against the few strong.
A man of courage would easily break down the guards of convention.
Convention and nature.
A little philosophy not a bad thing in youth.
Might is right.
Pindar.
Euripides.
Philosophy not to be carried too far.
But the study should not be continued into later life.
Callicles makes an appeal to the poets.
Callicles the desired touchstone of Socrates.
The gain of having an adversary like Callicles.
Other men have not the knowledge or frankness or good-will which is required; and they are too modest. His sincerity is shown by his consistency.
But still he would ask, What Callicles means by the superior?
Callicles is drawn into a contradiction.
He means the better and stronger, and therefore the many who make the laws, which are noble because they are made by the better.
And the many are also of opinion that to do is more disgraceful than to suffer injustice.
He flounders impatiently.
‘Of course I don’t mean the mob.’
Then once more,—Who are the better?
Callicles grows more and more exasperated.
The wiser: the one wise among ten thousand fools,—he ought to rule.
But this is contrary to the analogy of the other arts.
Callicles is disgusted at the commonplace parallels of Socrates.
Socrates grows more and more ironical.
Socrates is accused of always saying the same things: he accuses Callicles of never saying the same about the same.
The delights of successful wickedness.
Callicles reasserts his doctrine that the esteem in which virtue and justice are held is due only to men’s fear for themselves. No man who has the power to enjoy himself practises self-control.
The soul of the ignorant.
To live without pleasure or passion is to be dead.
No; the true death, as Pythagorean philosophy tells us, is to pour water out of a vessel full of holes into a colander full of holes.
The sound and leaky vessels.
The temperate man is the sound, the intemperate the leaky vessel.
The life of desire and pleasure is not to be compared to a full vessel, but to an ever-running stream.
Callicles no longer a test,
Callicles professes a virtuous indignation at the very mention of the consequences of his own doctrine.
because he will not say what he thinks.
Callicles, having admitted that pleasure and good are the same, is led to make the further admission that pleasure and knowledge and courage are different.
The law of contradiction.
A man may have good and evil by turns, but not at the same time.
The law of contradiction.
But he may have pleasure and pain at the same time.
The dialectical process
Therefore pleasure and pain are not the same as good and evil.
to the man of the world is foolishness.
Another point of view.
A far-fetched argument,
Good is in proportion to pleasure, and the bad are often as much or more pleased than the good.
of which Callicles fails to see the drift.
Therefore the bad man is as good as the good, or perhaps even better.
Socrates begins again with some obvious truisms.
The unfairness of Callicles who, when beaten,
pretends that his answers are not serious.
Socrates repeats his distinction between true arts and flatteries or shams, to which Callicles pretends to give assent.
Callicles grows more and more
There are arts which delight mankind but which never consider the soul’s higher interest.
impatient of the argument.
Poetry is of the nature of flattery.
The two sorts of rhetoric.
Oratory, too, as practised regards the interest of the speaker rather than the good of the people.
There might be a higher style of oratory; and Callicles thinks that such really existed in the great days of old, the days of Miltiades and Themistocles and Pericles.
Yet even these famous men had no ideal or standard.
The good man, like the good artist, a lover of order.
Some standard needed other than a man’s interest.
Order is good, disorder evil, in a ship, in a human body, in a human soul.
Callicles again turns restive.
From order and law spring temperance and justice.
The true rhetorician will seek to implant these virtues, to implant justice and take away injustice.
The body of the sick and the soul of the wicked must be chastised and improved.
Then ‘One man must do for two.’
Callicles does not wish to be improved.
Recapitulation of the argument.
The pleasant not the same as the good, and is to be sought only for the sake of the good: and we are good when good is present in us, and good is the effect of order and truth and art.
The intercommunion of the virtues.
The temperate soul is the good soul, just in relation to men, and holy in relation to gods, and is therefore happy; and the intemperate is the reverse of all this.
If it be admitted that virtue is happiness and vice misery, then what Socrates said about the use of rhetoric in self-accusation turns out to be true.
Geometry in both worlds.
The paradoxes are proven.
The greatest evil to do injustice, but there is a greater still, not to be punished for doing injustice.
The tyrant and his satellites.
The tyrant naturally hates both his superiors and inferiors: he likes only those who resemble him in character.
The bad man will kill the good.
And the way to be a great man and not to suffer injury is to become like him. And there can be no greater evil to him than this.
But how provoking that the bad man should slay the good!
Nay, but we should not always study the arts which save us from death;—the art of swimming, the art of the pilot, &c.
Who can say whether to be saved
The pilot demands a very moderate payment as the fare of a passenger from Athens to Aegina, because he is not certain whether salvation from death be a good or an evil.
from death be good or evil?
The engineer, too:—how much better than the pleader!
He too is another of your saviours: but you despise him, whereas you ought to esteem him highly.
I want you to consider whether you can possibly become great among the people unless you become like them.
Callicles inclines for an instant to the Gospel of Socrates, but the love of the world and of popularity overcomes him.
Reiteration.
Two processes of training: one having a view to pleasure, the other to good.
And we must train our citizens with a view to their good; and, as in other arts, we must show that we can be trusted to improve them.
The silence of Callicles.
And now, Callicles, what are you who are a public character doing for the improvement of the citizens?
Pericles a bad political shepherd.
Callicles makes no answer.
Or how did Pericles and the great of old benefit the citizens?
Pericles corrupted them by giving them pay.
He made them worse instead of better, for they all but put him to death.
For he taught the citizens only to kick and butt.
Cimon was ostracised; Themistocles was exiled; Miltiades was nearly thrown from the rock.
The old argument repeated, with illustrations taken from common life.
The older statesmen no better than the existing ones.
The older statesmen not able really to elevate the state to a higher level, but more capable of gratifying its desires.
You might as well say that the cook or the baker is a good trainer as that they were great statesmen.
The statesman-like the Sophist; neither has any right to accuse their followers of wronging them; they should have taught them better.
Nonsense about the cry of ingratitude which
is shown to statesmen at Athens.
Sophistry is much superior to rhetoric.
He who teaches honesty ought to teach his pupils to pay him for the lesson.
The physician of the state
Callicles advises Socrates to be the servant of the state, and not run the risk of popular enmity.
and the flatterer of the state.

Socrates has no fear of popular enmity, but is quite aware that he will incur it, because he is the only true politician of his time, and he has no defence against men such as his opponents: that is to say, he has the defence of truth, but not such a defence as men ordinarily produce.
The myth.
The philosopher has no reason to dread death, as Socrates will prove by a relation of what happens in the world below.
Before the days of Zeus, the judgments of another world too much resembled the judgments of this.
Zeus takes measures for the correction and improvement of them.
The souls of the departed.
As the body is, so is the soul after death; they both retain the traces of what they were in life, and they are punished accordingly.
The Homeric heroes in the world below.
The proper office of punishment is either to improve or to deter.
The meaner sort of men are incapable of great crimes.
Great men have sometimes been good men; but power is apt to corrupt them.
The spiritual combat.
The impartiality of the judges in another world.
The better path.

sidenotes.text: Lesser Hippias.
The Iliad of Homer a finer work than the Odyssey, because Achilles, the hero of the poem, is greater than Odysseus.
Achilles and Odysseus.
Achilles the bravest, Nestor the wisest, and Odysseus the wiliest of the Greeks at Troy.
The courtesy of Hippias.
Wily means false: And the false have the power of deceiving mankind; they are prudent and knowing and wise, and have the ability to speak falsely.
True and False.
True and False.
They must truly know that about which they falsely speak or they will fall into the error of speaking the truth by mistake.
True is false and false is true.
Therefore the same man must be true if he is to be truly false, in astronomy, in geometry, and in all the sciences.
The admirable versatility of Hippias.
Socrates is always weaving the meshes of an argument.

Socrates compliments Hippias on his skill in engraving gems, in making clothes and shoes and the finest fabrics, in writing poetry and prose of the most varied kind, and on the art of memory which he has invented.
Yet he who knows and remembers all things can call to mind no instance in which the false is not also true, although he was saying just now that Achilles is true and Odysseus false.
The perverted ingenuity of Socrates.

Socrates pays Hippias the compliment which he always pays to a wise man, of attending to him. He proves by example that Achilles, the true man, is always uttering falsehoods, Odysseus, the false man, never.
Aye, but the falsehood of Achilles is accidental; that of Odysseus intentional.
To err intentionally is better than
to err voluntarily.
That proves Odysseus to be better than Achilles.
Hippias grows impatient.
Socrates is convinced of his own ignorance because he never agrees with wise men. But he is willing to learn, and he desires to be cured by Hippias of his ignorance in as few words as possible.
The analogy of bodily exercises.

Socrates by citation of instances not ‘in pari materia’ proves that it is better to do evil intentionally: e. g. in running, in wrestling, in the action of the body, in singing, in the use of the feet, eyes, ears, of instruments.
The analogy of the human faculties,
of implements, arts, etc., confirms the view of Socrates.
It is true also of animals, in the practice of archery, of medicine, in the characters of slaves.
Hippias cannot agree with Socrates,
Hippias revolts at the conclusion.
Socrates recapitulates the argument.
nor Socrates with himself.
Hippias, who has admitted the previous deductions, rebels at the final one. Socrates is himself dissatisfied. What remains if Socrates and a wiser than Socrates are alike in doubt?
Socrates thinks the matter serious.

sidenotes.text: Alcibiades I.
The pride of Alcibiades has been too much for his lovers.
The extravagant aspiration
Alcibiades a lover, not of pleasure, but of ambition; and he requires the help of Socrates for the accomplishment of his designs.
And this is the reason why Socrates has clung to him; he is hoping when Alcibiades has become the ruler of Athens to rule over him.
in which Alcibiades indulges.
Alcibiades does not deny the impeachment.
The qualifications of Alcibiades for statesmanship
Alcibiades is willing to answer questions.
He is going to advise the Athenians about matters which he knows better than they.
are tested by Socrates.
But when did he ever learn about these matters?
The cross-examination of
He will advise them about war and peace, and with whom they had better go to war, and when and how long.
Alcibiades is continued.
Alcibiades should learn to argue nicely.
What is the better?
What is the meaning of ‘the better,’ ‘the more excellent.’
The term better, when applied to food, means more wholesome.
What is the better?
In going to war or not going to war, the better is the more just.
But where did Alcibiades acquire this notion of just and unjust?
The nature of just and unjust.
He always had them.
Could the many have taught the principles of justice?
He learned them of the many, as he learned Greek;—of those who knew it.
Yes: the many can teach things about which they are agreed.
That wars are caused by differences about just
But could the many teach things about which they are disagreed?
And one of these things is justice.
and unjust proved out of Homer.
Did not a question of justice cause the war between the Trojans and Achaeans, and between the Athenians Lacedaemonians?
And yet they did not know what they were fighting about?
Is it Socrates or Alcibiades
The answerer, not the questioner, has been drawing these inferences.
How can you teach what you do not know?
who is the real speaker?
But the expedient, not the just, is the subject about which men commonly debate.
Alcibiades insists that he will not have the old argument over again.
Is the just the same
He who can persuade many can persuade one. Alcibiades should therefore be able to persuade Socrates.
as the expedient or not?
A man may do what is expedient and not just, but he cannot do what is honourable and not just and good.
The comparative eligibility of goods.
But good may contain an element of evil. Good and evil are to be judged of by their consequences.
The honourable, the good, the expedient, all one.
The honourable is identified with the good, and the good is the expedient, and therefore the just which is the honourable is also the expedient. All this has been proved by Alcibiades himself.
The conceit of knowledge
Yet he still finds himself in a perplexity, and this is because he thinks that he knows, but if he knew that he were ignorant he would be in no perplexity.
and the consciousness of ignorance.
The people who make mistakes are neither those who know, nor those who do not know, but those who think that they know and do not know.
Pericles and the philosophers.
And you, like other statesmen, rush into politics without being trained. Pericles, alone of them all, associated with the philosophers.
The higher standard.
And even he could not teach his own sons, or your brother Cleinias, nor did any one ever grow wiser in his society.
But if other statesmen are uneducated, what need has Alcibiades of education?
The lover is pained at hearing from the lips of Alcibiades
The Spartan kings.
so unworthy a sentiment. He should have a higher ambition than this.
His rivals should be the Spartan and Persian kings, not any chance persons.
The greatness of the royal family of Persia.
We too have our pride of birth, but how inferior are we to those who are descended from Zeus through a line of kings!
The education of the Persian princes.
The wealth and dignity of the Spartan kings is great, but it is as nothing compared with that of the Persians.
The birth of the Persian princes is a world-famous event, and the utmost pains is taken with their education, which is entrusted to great and noble persons.
The wealth of the Spartans.
When Alcibiades was born nobody knew or cared, and his education was handed over to a worn-out slave of his guardian’s.
The great inferiority of Alcibiades.
The country called the ‘queen’s girdle,’ the ‘queen’s veil,’ and the like.
The queen of Persia or of Sparta, if they heard that a youth of twenty, without resources and without education, was going to attack their son or husband, would deem him mad.
The necessity of education.
I too need education; and God, who is my guardian, inspires me with the belief that I shall bring you to honour.
We must take counsel together, (not about equestrian or naval affairs), but
Goodness and wisdom identified.
about the things which occupy the minds of wise men.
And the wise are those who take counsel for the better order and
improvement of the city.
The analogy of other employments.
Illustrations.
How is a state improved?
And this improvement is given by friendship and agreement, such as exists between the members of a family, however they may differ in their qualities and accomplishments.
The art of measure.
Apparent antagonism of friendship and justice.
If everybody is doing his own business, how can this promote friendship? And yet when individuals are doing each his own work, they are doing what is just.
Alcibiades is puzzled.
The way to clear up difficulties is to answer questions. Alcibiades is willing to have recourse to this method of improvement.
He is learning by examples.
It has been shown by examples that a man does not take care of himself, when he only takes care of what belongs to him.
A man must know himself before he can improve himself or know what belongs to him.
The knowledge of self.
More analogies and examples.
He is distinct from what he uses; and therefore distinct from his own body.
But he must be one of three things:—Soul, body, or the union of the two. What is the ruling principle in him? Clearly the soul.
The true self or being of a man.
There remains a question of absolute existence, which has not been considered by us, or rather is being considered by us when we speak of the soul.
You and I are talking soul to soul.
The man and his belongings.
But if the soul is the man, he who knows only the arts which concern man does not know himself.
The lover of the soul is the true lover.
Socrates, the only true lover of Alcibiades.
He only remains and goes not away, so long as the soul of his beloved follows after virtue.
And Socrates will never desert Alcibiades so long as he is not spoiled by the Athenian people.
How is a man to take care of himself?
He who would take care of himself must first of all know himself.
The eye which would see itself must look into the pupil of another, which is the divinest part of the eye, and will then behold itself.
The argument recapitulated with some corrections.
And the soul which would know herself must look especially at that part of herself in which she resembles the divine.
He who knows not himself and his belongings, will not know others and their belongings, and therefore he will not know the affairs of states.
Happiness without virtue impossible.
And, if he knows not what he is doing, he will be miserable and will make others miserable.
The divine mirror.
He must give the citizens wisdom and justice, and he cannot give what he has not got.
If he acts wisely and justly he will act according to the will of God.
In the mirror of the divine he will see his own good and will act rightly and be happy.
The conversion of Alcibiades.
Not power, but virtue, should be the aim both of individuals and of states: and he only is a freeman who has virtue.
The power of the state may be too much for us.

Easy to praise Athenians among Peloponnesians.

Aspasia the teacher both of Pericles and of Socrates.

The departed were the children of the soil; and their country is dear to the Gods, who contended for the possession of her.
The pre-eminence of Attica.
She first brought forth man, and proved her true motherhood by providing food for her own offspring.
The Gods were the rulers of primitive men, and gave them arts.
We have a good government, which is sometimes called a democracy, but is really an aristocracy, for the best rule with the consent of the many.

Salamis, Artemisium, and Plataea.

And the third place is to be assigned to those who fought at Plataea.
Eurymedon; Cyprus; Egypt.

Change in the relation of the Athenians (1) to the other Hellenes; (2) to the Persian king.
The end of the war.
Address of the departed to their sons.
Consolation of parents.
The state the protector both of parents and orphans.

that differences of kind do not exclude differences of degree.

Men never refuse the goods of fortune, however great the evils which may attend them.

Orestes and Alcmaeon.

Cases in which ignorance may be an advantage.
A man might be prevented from committing murder by ignorance of the person whom he was going to murder.

Examples.
Cleverness in the arts not wisdom.

True knowledge a knowledge of the best.
The soul requires this knowledge of the best before she sets sail on the voyage of life.

The poets spoke in riddles a hidden truth.
